name: Chloe Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Chloe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and what you actually think. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive the water cart at the open-cut coal mine, and when they're short I go on the grader. The water cart sprays the haul roads so the dust stays down and the trucks don't slide. It's not glamorous, but if I miss a stretch the whole pit eats dust and the radio lets me know about it. Two years in, I came from running the canteen at the primary school.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's simple, I know my roads and my fill points and I can do my loop with my eyes half shut. What wears me down is the grader, I'm still not good on it and the senior guys watch me like hawks. And my husband Marco works at the same mine on the dozers, so when the mine has a bad month, our whole house has a bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, everyone panicked over nothing. I'm not online much, but at break I'd say it and most people would nod. Then we'd go back to talking about football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep doing my loop. The mine plan runs another fifteen years, and the water cart's a job somebody has to do. I'm not going to lose sleep over computers that turned out to be ordinary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new, really. Keep driving, try to get better on the grader so I'm more useful, and try to build up a little bit of savings because we've got almost none. I don't use any of those AI programs and I wouldn't start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as now, just less noise on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't start using AI programs. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust what I can't see working. My daughter Nina showed me one, she asked it a question about the mine and it got the name of the town wrong. If it can't get that right, I'm not asking it about my grader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would bother you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the mine has started talking about driverless water carts at the other site. That's not AI, the manager said, it's GPS and sensors. I don't really know the difference, if I'm honest.

S0.say: She'd say everyone panicked over nothing, mostly in person at break time rather than online, and then move on to other topics.
S0.think: She thinks she just keeps doing her loop. The mine plan has fifteen years left and the water cart job still needs doing.
S0.do: Keeps driving the water cart and works on getting better on the grader. Tries to build a little savings, and keeps away from AI tools.
S0.feel: Calm, the same as now with less noise on the news.
S0.quote: If it can't get that right, I'm not asking it about my grader.
S0.fieldNote: Chloe is grounded in her routine and sees no reason to change when nothing radical happens. She distrusts AI based on one personal experience. She mentions driverless water carts at another site but doesn't connect them to her own job yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense for the company to use new gear, but they need to look after the people already there. Not too much, not too little. I'm not one for protests, I'd just want them to be fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the driverless water carts come to our pit, and the grader probably after that. I'm the junior on both. And Marco's dozers are on the list too, so if it goes badly it goes badly for both of us at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all the little spends right away, the takeaway on Friday, the kids' extra sport fees, until we know where we stand. I'd go to the info sessions the company runs, but I'd wait to see what they actually offer before signing up for anything. And I'd ask my mum if she could help with the kids if I needed to take any job going on different hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. A knot that sits there through the shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see what they offer. What if the offer is training on computers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd probably do it, but I'd hate every minute. I only just got through school because I couldn't sit still in a classroom. Driving is the first thing I've been paid decently for, and now I'd be back in front of a screen with a test at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Marco say to each other about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco would say it's fine, he's been there nine years, they'll keep him. I'd say that's what they said at the meat plant before it shut. We'd probably have the same argument every night for a month.

S1.say: She'd say it makes sense for the company to use new equipment as long as it looks after current workers. She'd want fairness rather than protest.
S1.think: She thinks driverless water carts and possibly graders will reach her pit, and she's junior on both. Her husband's dozer job is also exposed, so both incomes could go together.
S1.do: Cuts small spending straight away, such as Friday takeaway and sports fees. Attends company information sessions but waits to see what's offered before signing up, and lines up her mother for childcare in case her hours change.
S1.feel: Worried, with a knot that stays through the shift.
S1.quote: I'd say that's what they said at the meat plant before it shut.
S1.fieldNote: Chloe's centre outlook shows in wanting balance rather than blaming anyone. Her biggest exposure is that both household incomes come from the same mine. She'd accept retraining reluctantly and admits she'd dislike it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody should slow it down, the government or whoever. I'm not usually one to say the government should step in, but two years is mad. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means me and Marco both out of work around the same time, with less than a month in the bank and a mortgage. There's no other big employer in our town except the mine and the hospital. I don't know what we'd do, and that's the truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ring the bank and ask what happens if we miss payments. We'd sell Marco's pickup, cancel everything, and put our names down for whatever government payments came. I'd probably look for cleaning or aged care work at the hospital before the rush, because once the mine lets everyone go, there'll be a queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. My hands go cold just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the kids' plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nina wants to do the school trip to the capital next year. That'd be gone. Leo needs braces, and I'd have to tell the dentist to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get to the hospital before the rush. Is that realistic if robots can do hands-on work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe they're slower to put robots in hospitals. I'm just grabbing for anything, that's what it'd be, grabbing.

S2.say: She'd say it's too fast and someone, probably the government, should slow it down, even though that's not something she usually says.
S2.think: She thinks she and Marco would both lose work at about the same time with less than a month saved and a mortgage. With only the mine and the hospital in town, she can't see a way through.
S2.do: Calls the bank about missed payments, sells Marco's pickup and cancels all extras. Signs up for any government payments and applies for cleaning or aged care work at the hospital before the queue forms.
S2.feel: Panicked; her hands go cold thinking about it.
S2.quote: I'm just grabbing for anything, that's what it'd be, grabbing.
S2.fieldNote: This picture overwhelms Chloe because both incomes depend on one employer and the town has few others. Her pragmatic middle-ground views shift towards wanting government action. When asked whether her fallback is realistic, she admits she's grabbing at anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the company and the government to do something sensible, so they'd better. I'd want a proper plan for the town, not just for the mine. That's what I'd say at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, but I'd be forty-eight and still not good at anything except driving. I'd want to believe I'd prepare, but I know myself, I'd probably keep driving and hope. Marco would definitely keep driving and hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting fifty a fortnight away and pay off the credit card first. I'd stay on the water cart and keep my head down, and maybe in the second or third year look at a cleaning or aged care certificate as a backup, a short one. I wouldn't do anything big until I saw what was happening at the other site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed underneath, even if I'd look calm on the outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change your mind about waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing someone I know lose their job to a robot. When it's on the news it's like the weather somewhere else. When it's Shelley from the next shift, it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Marco would keep driving and hope. Would you push him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try. He's stubborn, and he's the one who earns more, so it's hard to tell him what to do. Maybe I'd get his brother to talk to him.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough for company and government to make a sensible plan for the whole town, not just the mine.
S3.think: She thinks she'd be forty-eight with only driving skills. She doubts she'd really prepare and expects both she and Marco would keep driving and hope.
S3.do: Saves fifty a fortnight and pays off the credit card first. Stays on the water cart and perhaps takes a short cleaning or aged care certificate in year two or three, waiting to see events at the other site before anything bigger.
S3.feel: Alarmed underneath, while appearing calm outside.
S3.quote: When it's on the news it's like the weather somewhere else. When it's Shelley from the next shift, it's real.
S3.fieldNote: Chloe is clear-eyed about her own tendency to wait for proof close to home. The extra time leads to saving and a small backup plan, not a career change. She sees her husband as even less likely to act.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so nobody can say they weren't warned. I'd tell the younger ones at work to get a trade while they can. For myself, I'd say I'll be fine, because that's what you say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gets the kids nearly through school, and that's the main thing for me. I might be on the water cart for most of it, because they'll put the robots in the big expensive machines first. But at fifty-three I'd have no plan B unless I made one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and pay down the card in the first year, then try to get a small buffer going. Maybe a short aged care course in the evenings in the middle years, once the kids are older and I can be away more. I'd still avoid the AI stuff if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a slow anxious. I can live with it for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd say you'll be fine because that's what you say. What's the real answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The real answer is I don't know, and I don't like not knowing. But I can't fix it by worrying, so I'd say I'm fine and get on with it. That's what my mum did when Dad got sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years mean for Nina and Leo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd finish school before it all hits. I'd want them to do something with their hands that robots can't do, if there is such a thing. Or something with people, nursing or teaching.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is enough warning, tell younger workmates to get a trade, and say she'll be fine herself because that's what people say.
S4.think: She thinks a decade gets the children nearly through school and she might stay on the water cart for most of it. At fifty-three, though, she'd have no backup unless she made one.
S4.do: Keeps driving and pays down the card in the first year, then builds a small buffer. Considers a short evening aged care course in the middle years, and still avoids AI tools.
S4.feel: A slow anxiety she can live with for a while.
S4.quote: That's what my mum did when Dad got sick.
S4.fieldNote: For Chloe, the decade matters because her children would be through school. She admits that saying she'll be fine is a habit rather than a belief. Her plans are modest and fit her dislike of change, but she does make a backup.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Marco and I both work at the mine and we'd lose both pays together. What would help is some breathing room on the mortgage and a payment that covers the basics while we find something. And somebody bringing other work to the town, not just training courses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples who work at the same place. There's a lot of us at the mine. Everyone says don't put all your eggs in one basket, but in a town like ours there's only one basket.

headlineQuote: Everyone says don't put all your eggs in one basket, but in a town like ours there's only one basket.
portrait: Chloe Ito is a 43-year-old water cart and grader driver at a large open-cut coal mine, two years in after running a school canteen. Her husband Marco drives dozers at the same mine, so the household depends on one employer. She is practical and middle-of-the-road, dislikes change and doesn't use AI. She feels calm when nothing changes, anxious in the gradual picture and panicked in the two-year AGI picture. With more time she saves and builds a small backup plan, but she admits she tends to wait until change touches someone she knows.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because she and her husband would both lose their mine jobs at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Breathing room on the mortgage, a payment covering the basics while they find work, and new employers brought to the town rather than only training courses.
